purpose: Alosetron is used to treat severe irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea (IBS-D) in women who have had symptoms for at least 6 months and have not responded to other treatments. It helps reduce diarrhea, urgent bathroom trips, and belly pain. It is only approved for women because clinical studies were mainly done in women.
how_it_works: Your gut has special receptors called serotonin receptors that control how fast food moves through your intestines. Alosetron blocks one of these receptors, called the 5-HT3 receptor, which slows down movement in the bowel. This helps reduce cramping, urgency, and loose stools.
common_side_effects: The most common side effect is constipation, which can sometimes be serious. You might also experience nausea, stomach pain, or discomfort in your belly.
warnings: This medication has serious risks. It can cause severe constipation that may require hospitalization or surgery. It can also cause a rare but dangerous condition called ischemic colitis, where blood flow to the colon is reduced. Stop taking it right away and call your doctor if you have sudden or worsening stomach pain, blood in your stool, or new or worsening constipation. Because of these risks, only doctors who are enrolled in a special safety program can prescribe this medication.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose is 0.5 mg taken by mouth twice a day for the first 4 weeks. If you tolerate it well but still have symptoms, your doctor may increase the dose to 1 mg twice a day. If your symptoms do not improve after 4 weeks on the higher dose, the medication will be stopped.
